title: Japan Faces Hard Choices in Weaning off Russian Energy
gist: Japan, which imports over 97 percent of its LNG and nearly all its oil and coal, faces hard choices on weaning off Russian energy such as Sakhalin-II LNG after successive shocks from the Ukraine war and the Strait of Hormuz closure; the IEA forecasts Japanese electricity prices up 40 percent year-on-year in H2 2026 versus 25 percent for the EU.

insights.claim: LNG accounts for 30 percent of Japan's electricity generation, Japan imports more than 97 percent of its LNG, and its crude oil and coal supplies are almost 100 percent imported.
insights.speaker: Brian Wu
insights.so_what: Japan's extreme import dependence makes it a price-taker exposed to any LNG supply disruption; supports long-term LNG contracting demand.

insights.claim: Japan is one of the most energy-insecure countries in the world relative to the size of its population and economy.
insights.speaker: Brian Wu
insights.so_what: Energy security is a structural driver of Japanese policy on Russian projects, nuclear restarts and LNG deals.

insights.claim: Successive energy shocks from Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz have raised Japanese household costs and depressed growth.
insights.speaker: Brian Wu
insights.so_what: Energy costs are a drag on Japanese consumption and GDP; relevant to BOJ and JGB outlook.
insights.locator: Successive energy shocks produced by Russia

insights.claim: The International Energy Agency forecasts Japanese electricity prices in the second half of 2026 will surge 40 percent year-on-year, compared with only 25 percent for the European Union.
insights.speaker: Brian Wu
insights.so_what: Japan faces a sharper power-price shock than Europe, pressuring utilities, energy-intensive industry and household demand.

insights.claim: Weaning off Russian energy, including LNG from the Sakhalin-II project, poses hard trade-offs for Japan given its import dependence and elevated prices.
insights.speaker: Brian Wu
insights.so_what: Sakhalin-II offtake decisions affect Japanese buyers and global LNG balances; exit is costly while Hormuz supply is disrupted.
